analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling in the Atlantic Ocean.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in April 2009 with 3 Senate backers, it sat in the Energy Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The COAST Anti-Drilling Act would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Secretary from ever leasing the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas for oil, gas, or mineral drilling [S2, S3]. That would make the ban permanent in law, rather than leaving it to whatever administration is in office. The bill was introduced by Sen. Robert Menendez of New Jersey with Sen. Frank Lautenberg and one other Democrat cosponsoring, read twice, and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on April 2, 2009 [S1, S3, S5]. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic — tourism businesses, commercial and recreational fishing, beach towns from New Jersey to New England and the mid-Atlantic — benefit from a permanent legal shield against offshore drilling accidents and the routine pollution that comes with drilling platforms. Ordinary taxpayers also avoid exposure to the cleanup and economic damage costs that a spill in those waters would impose.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal towns, tourism and fishing

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or minerals in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas [S2, S3].
Because the ban would be written into statute, it could not be undone by a future administration's leasing plan, unlike a temporary presidential withdrawal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose potential access to any oil and gas reserves under the Atlantic outer continental shelf, and the federal government forgoes potential lease revenue. To the extent domestic production matters to supply, the ban forecloses one region of potential development.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Atlantic leases

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently forecloses energy development and lease revenue from a large offshore region, removing any option to revisit the question as technology or energy conditions change [S2, S3].
A ban does not itself lower fuel prices; any oil not produced in the Atlantic comes from other domestic or foreign sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Atlantic coastal states, the protection outweighs the cost: a single spill can devastate tourism and fisheries for years, while the drilling revenue would mostly flow to leaseholders and the Treasury. The real cost is the foregone option value of energy development — the bill settles that tradeoff permanently and in one direction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Menendez introduced the bill on April 2, 2009, with Sen. Lautenberg named as an original cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day [S3, S5].
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill — 2 of 58 Senate Democrats — and no Republican cosponsors joined [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill during the 111th Congress, and it died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off: the statutory ban never became law, so Atlantic waters remained available to future leasing plans. Atlantic coastal communities, meanwhile, were left without the permanent legal protection the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling and referred it to the Energy Committee.

for.name: 2 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no additional senators joined beyond the sponsor's original group.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, leaving it to die without action.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so no party split is recorded; it had only Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, and the decisive inaction was a Democratic-chaired committee.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred them from leasing and developing the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas. Their interest in access runs against coastal communities that would bear the spill and pollution risk.

A permanent ban protects the beaches, fisheries, and coastal economies that offshore drilling accidents and routine platform pollution would put at risk. These businesses gain together with the residents they serve.
